description: Take the Shanghai Tower apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the twisted supertall: a 120-degree spiral that tamed the typhoon winds of Pudong.

hotspots.text: The outer skin is a rounded triangle in plan, twisting 120 degrees from base to tip. Wind-tunnel tests showed the spiral cuts wind loads by 24 percent.
hotspots.title: The 120-degree twist

hotspots.text: A 1,000-tonne tuned mass damper near the top counteracts sway; the tower can move up to a metre in high winds.
hotspots.title: Tuned mass damper

hotspots.text: Each of the nine zones has a sky lobby set in the cavity between the two glass skins, with planted garden atriums open to tenants.
hotspots.title: Sky lobbies

hotspots.text: The roughly 90-by-90-foot concrete core carries the tower, tied to twelve composite super-columns by outrigger trusses.
hotspots.title: Concrete core

hotspots.text: The circular inner curtain wall encloses the occupied floors; the triangular outer wall stands free of it, creating the double-skin cavity.
hotspots.title: Double skin

hotspots.text: The glass crown closes the 632 m tip, the second-tallest building in the world at its 2015 completion.
hotspots.title: The crown

intro: In Pudong, where Shanghai built a financial district out of farmland in a single generation, the tallest tower does not stand straight. It twists. The Shanghai Tower spirals 120 degrees as it climbs 632 metres, and the twist is not decoration: it is how the building survives the typhoon.

sections.body: Shanghai Tower Construction and Development built the tower between 2008 and 2015 to a Gensler design led by Marshall Strabala and Jun Xia, with Thornton Tomasetti as structural engineer. At 632 metres and 128 floors it was the third building ever to pass 600 metres, the tallest in China and the second tallest in the world on completion. The $2.4 billion tower completed the Lujiazui trio alongside the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center.
sections.heading: A twist in Pudong

sections.body: More than a dozen models were tested in a Toronto wind tunnel before Gensler settled on the final form: an asymmetric, tapering spiral with rounded corners and a deep notch running its length. Together the twist and the taper cut wind loads by 24 percent, which meant less steel and concrete were needed to stiffen the building, reportedly saving $58 million. The tower still sways up to a metre in high winds; a 1,000-tonne tuned mass damper near the top keeps that motion comfortable.
sections.heading: Shaped by the wind

sections.body: The tower is really nine vertical buildings stacked inside one twisting skin. Each zone runs 12 to 15 storeys and has its own sky lobby, and the zones are wrapped in two separate curtain walls: a circular inner wall around the occupied floors and the cam-shaped triangular outer wall. The cavity between them holds garden atriums at every zone, so every tenant is never more than a few floors from planted public space. The 20,000-plus triangular glass panels of the outer skin make it the tallest double-facade building in the world.
sections.heading: Nine towers in one

sections.body: The tower runs on some of the fastest elevators ever installed, reaching 20.5 metres per second and covering the trip to the observation deck in 55 seconds. The J Hotel occupies floors 84 to 110, the second-highest hotel in the world when it opened. Below grade, five levels hold retail, parking for 1,800 cars and services; above, the five-storey podium holds shops, a bank and a multifunction hall. LEED Platinum and China three-star green building certifications followed.
sections.heading: The vertical city

sections.body: Mission: Impossible III (2006) put Shanghai on the action-movie map, but the Shanghai Tower cannot appear in it: the film predates the tower by nearly a decade, and its Shanghai leap was staged in a hangar with CGI anyway. The skyline Tom Cruise swings through belongs to the older trio of the Oriental Pearl Tower, Jin Mao and the Shanghai World Financial Center. The real Shanghai Tower arrived too late for that franchise and just in time for the next one: it now anchors establishing shots of modern Shanghai wherever a production needs the definitive 21st-century skyline.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

sources: Historical facts adapted from Wikipedia ("Shanghai Tower", CC BY-SA), the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, Gensler project pages, and AFP reporting on the 2015 opening. Cultural appearances verified against film production coverage.

timeline.text: Construction begins in Lujiazui, Pudong, to Gensler's twisting design.
The tower receives China's three-star green building design certificate.
CTBUH marks completion at 632 m and 128 storeys: tallest in China, second tallest in the world.
The tower opens to the public; the observation deck and J Hotel come online.

title: Shanghai Tower
